topics.title: Matter and its properties
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
topics.concept: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It exists mainly as solid, liquid or gas, and is classified as pure substances (elements, compounds) or mixtures (homogeneous such as alloys, heterogeneous such as muddy water).

subtopics.title: Physical properties; intensive vs extensive; elements, compounds, mixtures
subtopics.concept: Intensive properties (temperature, density, melting point, colour) do not depend on the amount of matter; extensive properties (mass, volume) do. Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds contain elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio (e.g. dry ice = CO₂); mixtures have variable composition (alloys such as brass, bronze, solder, mild steel).

subtopics.title: States of matter and fluids
subtopics.concept: Solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of the container; gases fill the container. Liquids and gases can flow, so both are called fluids. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

subtopics.title: Mixtures and alloys
subtopics.concept: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other elements: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), solder (Sn + Pb), mild steel (Fe + C), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

subtopics.title: Separation techniques
subtopics.concept: Sedimentation: coarse particles settle under gravity. Decantation: pouring off the clear liquid. Filtration: separating an insoluble solid with a filter. Evaporation and distillation use differences in boiling point.

topics.title: Atomic structure
topics.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
topics.concept: Atoms contain protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons in shells. Atomic number Z = number of protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. Ions form when atoms lose or gain electrons; the number of protons never changes.

subtopics.title: Electrons, ions, valence electrons, isoelectronic species
subtopics.concept: Electrons in an ion = Z − charge. Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons (e.g. Ar, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, S²⁻ all have 18). Valence electrons are the outer-shell electrons; nonmetals gain 8 − (valence electrons) electrons to form anions, e.g. N (5 valence e⁻) forms N³⁻ in Na₃N. Anions are larger than their atoms; cations smaller.

subtopics.title: Isotopes and average atomic mass
subtopics.concept: Isotopes have the same Z but different numbers of neutrons. Average atomic mass = Σ(fractional abundance × isotopic mass); it lies closer to the most abundant isotope (e.g. Cu ≈ 63.55 u).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

topics.title: Chemical bonding and intermolecular forces
topics.unit: G9 Unit 2 / G10 Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
topics.concept: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer from metals to nonmetals; covalent bonds by sharing electrons between nonmetals. Covalent bonds are polar when the atoms have different electronegativities. Intermolecular forces (dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonds) act between molecules.

subtopics.title: Ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds
subtopics.concept: Metal + nonmetal → ionic (e.g. RbCl, K₂O). Nonmetal + nonmetal → covalent. Coordinate covalent bond: both shared electrons come from one atom (e.g. NH₄⁺).

subtopics.title: Polar and nonpolar covalent bonds
subtopics.concept: Identical atoms share electrons equally (H₂, Cl₂, O₂: nonpolar). Different nonmetals share unequally and the more electronegative atom becomes δ− (HCl, H₂O, HF: polar).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

subtopics.title: Dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding
subtopics.concept: Nonpolar molecules attract by dispersion forces; polar molecules (HCl) by dipole–dipole forces; polar + nonpolar by dipole–induced dipole forces. Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction when H is bonded to F, O or N (HF, H₂O, NH₃). Molecular crystals held by these weak forces have low melting points.

topics.title: Formulas, the mole and stoichiometry
topics.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations
topics.concept: Chemical formulas are written by balancing ionic charges (criss-cross). One mole contains 6.02×10²³ particles; n = m/M; particles = n × NA. Balanced equations give mole ratios for stoichiometric calculations.

subtopics.title: Writing formulas with polyatomic ions
subtopics.concept: Criss-cross the charges and use brackets when more than one polyatomic ion is needed: Al³⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Al₂(SO₄)₃; Ca²⁺ + PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

subtopics.title: Mole, molar mass, number of particles
subtopics.concept: n = m/M. Number of molecules = n × 6.02×10²³; number of atoms = molecules × atoms per molecule (include water of crystallization, e.g. ZnSO₄·7H₂O has 27 atoms). For equal masses, the substance with the smallest molar mass has the most molecules.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations
Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations
Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

subtopics.title: Mole ratios from balanced equations
subtopics.concept: Balance first, then use coefficients as mole ratios, e.g. 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O: 1 mol C₂H₂ gives 2 mol CO₂ (88 g).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

subtopics.title: Balancing (redox) equations
subtopics.concept: Balance atoms other than H and O first; for redox reactions make electrons lost = electrons gained (oxidation-number method), then balance O with H₂O and finally H.

textbook_refs.section: 2.1.4 Writing and Balancing Simple Redox Equations

topics.title: Periodic table and periodic trends
topics.concept: Across a period: atomic radius decreases, ionization energy and electronegativity increase, nonmetallic character increases. Down a group: the opposite. Group 1 alkali metals react with water to form strong bases.

subtopics.title: Groups and periods; alkali metals
subtopics.concept: The group of a main-group element equals its number of valence electrons. Alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb…) have 1 valence electron, form M⁺ ions and react with water: 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂ (solution becomes basic).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

textbook_refs.section: 4.2.3 Preparation of bases – active metal + water

subtopics.title: Trends in radius, IE, electronegativity, metallic character
subtopics.concept: Nuclear charge increases across a period while shielding stays similar, so electrons are held more tightly: radius ↓, IE ↑, EN ↑. Down a group, new shells are added: radius ↑, IE ↓, metallic character ↑.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

textbook_refs.section: 1.4.1 Trends in atomic and ionic radii

subtopics.title: Ionization energy
subtopics.concept: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. It depends on distance from the nucleus, nuclear charge, shielding by inner shells and the type of electron. Removing an electron from a noble-gas core (e.g. Na⁺ → Na²⁺) needs a very large energy; He has the highest first IE.

topics.title: Solutions and their properties
topics.concept: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. Concentration can be expressed as molarity (mol/L), molality (mol/kg) or normality (equivalents/L). Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles.

subtopics.title: Solubility; saturated solutions
subtopics.concept: A saturated solution contains the maximum dissolved solute at that temperature. Solubility is usually given in g per 100 g (or 100 mL) of water at a stated temperature.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_refs.section: Room temperature taken as 25 °C (Unit 1 review Q6a)

subtopics.title: Solubility data and crystallization
subtopics.concept: When a saturated solution is cooled, the mass of crystals formed = solubility at the higher temperature − solubility at the lower temperature (per 100 g water).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_refs.section: Room temperature taken as 25 °C (Unit 1 review Q6a)

subtopics.title: Molarity, normality, equivalent mass
subtopics.concept: Molarity M = moles of solute / litres of solution. Normality N = equivalents / litres = M × n, where n = replaceable H⁺ (acids) or OH⁻ (bases). Equivalent mass = molar mass / n (e.g. H₂SO₄ 49 g, Na₂CO₃ 53 g). Titration: MaVa·na = MbVb·nb.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_refs.section: Room temperature taken as 25 °C (Unit 1 review Q6a)

subtopics.title: Colligative properties
subtopics.concept: Adding solute lowers the vapour pressure and freezing point and raises the boiling point and osmotic pressure. ΔTf = Kf·m (multiply by the number of ions for ionic solutes, e.g. MgCl₂ → 3 particles). Water: Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol, Kb = 0.52 °C·kg/mol.

topics.title: Acids, bases and salts
topics.concept: Acids produce H⁺ (H₃O⁺) in water, bases produce OH⁻. Basicity = number of replaceable H. Salts form in neutralization. pH = −log[H⁺]; at 25 °C [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1×10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14.

subtopics.title: Properties, basicity, neutralization uses
subtopics.concept: Monoprotic: HCl, HNO₃, CH₃COOH (only the –COOH H is acidic). Diprotic: H₂SO₄, H₂CO₃, H₂S. Triprotic: H₃PO₄. Acidic soil is treated with lime/limestone (CaCO₃); basic soil with ammonium sulphate.

4.4.3 General Properties of Salts – Table 4.4 Solubility of salts
4.3 Neutralization – reducing acidity or alkalinity of soil

subtopics.title: pH, pOH and Kw
subtopics.concept: [H₃O⁺] = 1×10⁻¹⁴/[OH⁻]. For strong bases count all OH⁻: 0.05 M Ba(OH)₂ → [OH⁻] = 0.10 M → pOH 1 → pH 13.

subtopics.title: Titration and indicators
subtopics.concept: In titration a standard solution is added from a burette until the indicator changes colour (end point). Indicators are weak acids/bases that change colour by gaining/losing H⁺: phenolphthalein colourless (acid)/pink (base); methyl orange pink/yellow; litmus red/blue.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_refs.section: Room temperature taken as 25 °C (Unit 1 review Q6a)

subtopics.title: Solubility of salts
subtopics.concept: All nitrates and all Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ salts are soluble. Only Na, K and NH₄ carbonates are soluble. AgCl and PbSO₄, BaSO₄ are insoluble; CaSO₄ is only slightly soluble.

textbook_refs.section: 4.4.3 General Properties of Salts – Table 4.4 Solubility of salts

topics.title: Energy and chemical reactions
topics.concept: Thermochemical equations show heat changes. Exothermic: heat written with the products, as '− heat' with the reactants, or ΔH < 0. Heats of fusion, vaporization, formation, solution, neutralization and combustion are defined per mole.

subtopics.title: Thermochemical equations and heat calculations
subtopics.concept: Balance the equation first; the heat value belongs to the mole amounts in the balanced equation. Heat for x mol = (x / coefficient) × ΔH. Heat of fusion: heat to melt 1 mol of solid at its melting point; heat of vaporization: 1 mol liquid → vapour at its boiling point.

topics.title: Reaction rates and equilibrium
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
topics.concept: Reactions need collisions with correct orientation and at least the activation energy. Rate increases with temperature, concentration, pressure, surface area and catalysts. At equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts.

subtopics.title: Collision theory and factors affecting rate
subtopics.concept: Activation energy is the minimum collision energy needed for reaction. Higher temperature increases the rate of ALL reactions (exothermic or endothermic). Smaller particles = larger surface area = faster. Catalysts lower the activation energy; inhibitors slow reactions.

subtopics.title: Le Chatelier's principle
subtopics.concept: If a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, it shifts to relieve the stress. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction (reverse for exothermic reactions); increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it

topics.title: Redox reactions and electrolysis
topics.concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number); reduction is gain (decrease). The oxidizing agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidized. Electrolysis uses electric current to drive non-spontaneous reactions; Faraday's laws relate charge to mass deposited.

subtopics.title: Oxidation numbers, oxidizing and reducing agents
subtopics.concept: Rules: element = 0; O = −2; H = +1 (with nonmetals); group 1 = +1; sum = charge. Example: S in NaHSO₄ = +6. In 2HNO₃ + 3SO₂ + 2H₂O → 3H₂SO₄ + 2NO, HNO₃ (N +5 → +2) is the oxidizing agent and SO₂ (S +4 → +6) the reducing agent.

textbook_refs.section: 2.1.4 Writing and Balancing Simple Redox Equations

subtopics.title: Electrolysis and preferential discharge
subtopics.concept: Electrolysis: decomposition of an electrolyte by electric current. Which ion is discharged depends on (1) position in the electrochemical series, (2) concentration and (3) nature of the electrodes. Cathode: reduction; anode: oxidation.

textbook_refs.section: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions – preferential discharge (Tables 2.2, 2.3)

subtopics.title: Faraday's laws
subtopics.concept: Q = I × t. Mass deposited m = (A/(Z·F)) × I × t, with F = 96 500 C/mol and Z = electrons per ion (Cu²⁺: Z = 2).

topics.title: Nonmetals and industrial processes
topics.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Important industrial processes: Haber (ammonia from N₂ + 3H₂, iron catalyst), Ostwald (nitric acid from ammonia), Contact (sulphuric acid via SO₃), Frasch (extraction of sulphur with superheated water and hot air).

subtopics.title: Nitrogen, sulphur and their compounds
subtopics.concept: Sulphur occurs free in underground deposits and is extracted by the Frasch process; it has rhombic and monoclinic allotropes. Ammonia is a colourless, pungent, very soluble basic gas.

subtopics.title: Industrial processes
subtopics.concept: Haber → NH₃; Ostwald → HNO₃; Contact → H₂SO₄; Frasch → S.

topics.title: Metals and metallurgy
topics.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Metallurgy is the science and technology of separating metals from their ores. Unreactive metals (Au, Ag, Pt, Cu) occur native; others as ores: bauxite (Al), haematite/magnetite (Fe), galena (Pb), chalcopyrite CuFeS₂ (Cu).

subtopics.title: Ores, roasting, calcination, reduction
subtopics.concept: Roasting: heating a sulphide ore in excess air → oxide + SO₂. Calcination: heating a carbonate ore in limited air → oxide + CO₂. The oxide is then reduced, e.g. ZnO + C → Zn + CO.

topics.title: Behaviour of gases
topics.concept: Gas laws: Boyle P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (constant T), Charles V/T constant, Avogadro (22.4 L/mol at STP), ideal gas law PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K. Density d = PM/RT. Gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure.

subtopics.title: Gas laws and calculations
subtopics.concept: Convert °C to K (+273) and mL to L. Molar mass from STP data: M = d × 22.4 or M = m × 22.4 / V(L). At constant T, expansion lowers the pressure; average kinetic energy depends only on temperature.

textbook_refs.section: 5.3 The Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases

subtopics.title: Kinetic molecular theory
subtopics.concept: Postulates: tiny particles with negligible volume; constant random straight-line motion; perfectly elastic collisions; no intermolecular forces; average kinetic energy ∝ absolute temperature. Real gases deviate at low T and high P.

textbook_refs.section: 5.3 The Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases

topics.title: Shapes of molecules and crystals
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
topics.concept: VSEPR: electron pairs around the central atom repel and get as far apart as possible. Crystals are classified into seven crystal systems by unit-cell edges and angles, and by bonding type (ionic, covalent, molecular, metallic).

subtopics.title: VSEPR shapes
subtopics.concept: 2 pairs linear (CO₂); 3 bonding pairs trigonal planar (BF₃, AlCl₃, each C in C₂H₄); 4 bonding pairs tetrahedral (CH₄); 3 bonding + 1 lone pair trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); 2 bonding + 2 lone pairs bent (H₂O). A double bond counts as one pair.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

subtopics.title: Crystal systems and types of crystals
subtopics.concept: Cubic a = b = c, all 90°; tetragonal a = b ≠ c, all 90°; orthorhombic a ≠ b ≠ c, all 90°; triclinic a ≠ b ≠ c and α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90°. Molecular crystals (ice, solid Ne) have the lowest melting points; covalent network crystals (diamond) the highest.

topics.title: Organic chemistry
topics.concept: Hydrocarbons are saturated (alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) or unsaturated (alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, aromatics). Functional groups define families: alcohols –OH, aldehydes –CHO, ketones –CO–, acids –COOH, esters –COO–, amides –CONH₂.

subtopics.title: General organic chemistry
subtopics.concept: Organic compounds are carbon compounds classified by carbon skeleton and functional group.

textbook_refs.section: 2.3.5 Organic Polymers – addition polymerization, Table of thermoplastics
2.3.2 Carboxylic Acids – reaction with active metals

subtopics.title: Alkanes, alkenes, alkynes; classification of carbon atoms
subtopics.concept: A carbon bonded to 1, 2, 3 or 4 other carbons is primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary (3-methylpentane has a tertiary carbon). Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

subtopics.title: Functional groups
subtopics.concept: CH₂O (methanal) is the simplest aldehyde; CH₃COCH₃ is a ketone.

subtopics.title: Alcohols
subtopics.concept: Primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols to ketones; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation. Alcohols react with Na to give alkoxides + H₂.

subtopics.title: Carboxylic acids
subtopics.concept: IUPAC names: alkane −e + oic acid (HCOOH methanoic acid = formic acid; CH₃COOH ethanoic acid = acetic acid). Acids react with active metals to give salts + H₂: 2CH₃CH₂COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂COONa (sodium propanoate) + H₂.

textbook_refs.section: 2.3.2 Carboxylic Acids – reaction with active metals

subtopics.title: Esters and amides
subtopics.concept: Ester RCOOR′ is named alkyl (R′) + acid-oate: CH₃(CH₂)₄COOCH₂CH₃ = ethyl hexanoate. Amides: alkane −e + amide, carbonyl carbon = C1: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CONH₂ = 3-methylbutanamide.

subtopics.title: IUPAC nomenclature
subtopics.concept: Find the longest chain containing the functional group, number from the end nearest the functional group, name branches with position numbers.

subtopics.title: Isomers
subtopics.concept: Isomers have the same molecular formula (and molar mass) but different structures: the butanols C₄H₁₀O all have M = 74 g/mol, whereas butanal C₄H₈O has 72 g/mol.

subtopics.title: Polymers and plastics
subtopics.concept: Addition polymers form from alkenes (polythene, PVC from vinyl chloride, polystyrene, Teflon from CF₂=CF₂) – thermoplastics. Condensation polymers eliminate small molecules (nylon, polyester, Bakelite, urea–methanal). Thermosetting plastics are heat resistant and cannot be remoulded.

textbook_refs.section: 2.3.5 Organic Polymers – addition polymerization, Table of thermoplastics
2.3.5 Organic Polymers – addition vs condensation, thermoplastics table

subtopics.title: Soaps and detergents
subtopics.concept: Saponification: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol. Salting out: adding concentrated NaCl makes the soap separate as curds from the glycerol solution.

textbook_refs.section: 2.3.4 Soaps and Detergents – preparation of soap

topics.title: Nuclear chemistry
topics.concept: Unstable nuclei decay by α (A − 4, Z − 2), β⁻ (Z + 1) or γ emission. Half-life is the time for half of a sample to decay. Transmutation changes one element into another. Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei. Mass lost is converted to energy: ΔE = Δmc².

subtopics.title: Decay, half-life, transmutation, fission and fusion
subtopics.concept: Remaining mass = initial × (1/2)ⁿ, n = time/half-life (same time units). Nuclear equations must balance mass numbers and atomic numbers, e.g. ²³⁹₉₂U + ⁴₂He → ²⁴²₉₄Pu + ¹₀n (transmutation of U to Pu).

textbook_refs.section: 3.1.3 Types of Radioactive Decay – alpha decay
3.3.1 The Power of the Nucleus – ΔE = Δmc², mass defect of deuterium

subtopics.title: Mass defect and binding energy
subtopics.concept: Mass defect Δm = mass of products − mass of reactants (negative: mass lost). Energy ΔE = Δm c², with Δm in kg and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s gives joules. For p + n → ²H (masses in the exam) Δm = −7.5×10⁻³⁰ kg, E = 6.75×10⁻¹³ J.

textbook_refs.section: 3.3.1 The Power of the Nucleus – ΔE = Δmc², mass defect of deuterium
